name: Daria Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. We keep your answers confidential. What is a normal day on the lines?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a crew building and repairing power lines for the electricity company. My two-year technical diploma taught me the drawings, and enough years on poles taught me when a drawing has missed something. Before any climb I want the isolation repeated back to me, which can irritate a hurried dispatcher. At home there are two school-age children, my partner and a mortgage, so the usual pay and a few months of savings need careful handling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the practical job is much the same. A form might come back faster, but no routine AI can decide whether the line we are touching has been isolated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not use AI tools, and I do not plan to start for a small paperwork gain. We have between one and six months saved, which helps, but the mortgage means I still want every dependable shift. A faster work order cannot tell my line crew whether a power line is isolated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my crew on the same check sequence and ask the depot clerk to flag any automated work order as such. In the first year I would continue putting fifty from each paid callout into our emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my job, though I still watch the mortgage balance. This picture does not change the work that earns my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you do with a flagged work order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will compare the pole address and isolation detail with what the crew sees on site. I would send it back for correction if the numbers do not match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a month has no callouts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then no fifty goes into savings from callouts that month. We would pay the usual bills and keep the existing emergency money for a real gap.

say: A **quicker** work order does not replace isolation checks on a power line.
I would **continue** the crew’s established field sequence.
think: My **savings** cover a few months, yet the mortgage still depends on regular shifts.
I **see** no reason to learn an AI tool for a minor form change.
do: **Keep** the crew’s isolation checks and verify flagged work orders on site.
**Save** fifty from each actual paid callout during the first year.
feel: **Mostly** calm about my job, while mindful of the mortgage.
S0.quote: A faster work order cannot tell my line crew whether a power line is isolated.
fieldNote: She **uses** no AI tools and regards field checks as the source of authority.
Her **moderate** cushion helps, while new saving depends on actual paid callouts.

steps.text: Keep crew isolation checks and verify flagged work orders on site
Save fifty from each paid callout into emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say planning software may shorten depot queues, but a field crew must be allowed to refuse a wrong sequence. I would ask the company to name the person who corrects a dangerous dispatch instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office work may shrink before repairs do, but tighter schedules could make my team lead role a target when hours are counted. There are some nearby lineworker jobs, not enough that I would throw away a steady wage. A dispatch screen cannot take responsibility when my power line crew finds the wrong pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record each delayed isolation and incorrect pole address for two months and give the depot manager the list. During the first year I would ask for a written correction process and keep taking the normal repair shifts while its safety is proved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I can picture pressure on the crew even if the work remains. I do not want an untried system making the timetable for a broken line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your list need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Each entry needs the order number, wrong instruction, actual hazard and minutes lost correcting it. I want a manager to answer the evidence rather than my opinion about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the planning tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not while the company is still finding its mistakes. I would inspect the work order it produces and keep the crew on the manual site checks.

say: **Planning** software may help dispatch, but crews need a named correction contact.
**Field** teams must retain authority to refuse unsafe repair sequences.
think: **Office** tasks change first, yet tighter schedules could squeeze lead hours and field judgment.
**Some** nearby openings exist, but I will not abandon a dependable wage without proof.
do: **Log** wrong pole addresses and delayed isolations for two months.
**Ask** depot manager for a written dispatch correction process.
**Keep** normal repair shifts while new schedules are tested.
feel: **Anxious** about time pressure and unsafe instructions, though my job remains useful.
S1.quote: A dispatch screen cannot take responsibility when my power line crew finds the wrong pole.
fieldNote: Her **concern** is responsibility for wrong instructions, rather than immediate robot replacement.
She **refuses** to use the planning tool personally but will inspect its field outputs.

steps.text: Log dispatch errors and submit records to depot manager
Keep normal power line repair shifts while schedules are tested

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew full thinking AI by 2028 may rewrite the plan, and capable robots around 2031 may attempt the climb. I would demand a signed human isolation check before any robot crosses onto a live site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crew could lose callout hours once a robot can repair the easy faults, and that would take a large piece of household income. We have a few months saved, not years, and the children and mortgage leave little room for an early mistake. My power line crew cannot sign off a robot climb with a family mortgage hanging on the same shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month my partner and I would stop booking our usual paid weekend trip and put the freed amount toward ordinary bills. Before 2028 my crew and I would bring a signed-check proposal to the company safety meeting; after thinking AI arrives I would compare the lead vacancies at nearby electricity companies if our callout hours actually fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and angry at the thought of workers being asked to bless an unsafe shortcut. I can act, but I cannot make a robot safe by wishing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the signed check work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A named crew lead would confirm the isolation and mark the pole on the work sheet before a robot moves. I would want that authority written down and paid as part of the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes another vacancy worth taking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a written offer with at least our current pay and a sensible journey from home. I would not uproot the children or quit on a rumour.

say: **Thinking** AI may change the plan by 2028, but robots around 2031 need signed human isolation checks.
I would **take** a written safety proposal to the company meeting.
think: **Robot** repair could cut callout hours and a large part of family income.
A **few** months of savings will not cover long disruption to mortgage payments.
do: **Cancel** the planned paid weekend trip to preserve household cash.
**Compare** nearby lead vacancies after 2028 only if callout hours fall.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours and angry about possible safety shortcuts.
S2.quote: My power line crew cannot sign off a robot climb with a family mortgage hanging on the same shift.
fieldNote: She **fears** a possible callout loss but still has actions and a few months of savings.
The **cancelled** trip is spending foregone, not new money saved from wages.

steps.text: Cancel planned paid weekend trip and protect ordinary bills
Present signed isolation check proposal with crew at company safety meeting
Compare nearby lead vacancies if callout hours fall after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 for thinking AI and 2034 for capable robots gives the company time to put actual crews into field trials. I would keep experienced lead workers on each isolation check until the machine has proved itself over many repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could see a paid safety inspection post for someone with my diploma, though I do not want to become the person tapping approval on a screen. The mortgage is still there, and any new post has to pay at least what line work brings home. A line inspection job should put my boots beside a damaged pole, not only my name on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the company for written details of its field inspection duties and pay. If it offers paid hands-on training and posts a local inspection role at no lower pay, I would take the course before 2031 and apply in the first year after full thinking AI arrives; otherwise I would keep leading repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with more time to judge real work. I would learn a new inspection duty when the evidence and pay are there, not on a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as hands-on training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need supervised checks on damaged crossarms, wet poles and wrong isolation markings. A video of a clean yard would not qualify me to approve a field repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A role that only reviews a screen, or one that pays less than my current wage, would stop me. I would remain with my crew while we still have repair work.

say: **Several** years allow proper field trials before robots work power lines around 2034.
**Experienced** leads should keep signed isolation authority during testing.
think: A **paid** inspection role may fit my diploma if it includes real site checks.
I **cannot** trade steady line wages for a lower paid screen approval job.
do: **Request** written inspection duties and pay this year.
**Take** paid hands-on inspection course before 2031 if suitable local post exists.
**Apply** after 2031 only if local inspection role pays at least current wage.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to judge evidence and pay before changing work.
S3.quote: A line inspection job should put my boots beside a damaged pole, not only my name on a screen.
fieldNote: Her **slow** adoption becomes a conditional willingness to train on physical safety tasks.
The **course** and application depend on paid field training and an actual local role.

steps.text: Take paid hands-on inspection course before 2031 if suitable local post exists
Apply after 2031 if inspection role pays at least current wage
Keep crew lead shifts if suitable paid inspection path is absent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger workers a decade before thinking AI and another three years before robots is enough to learn the old trade properly. I would keep practical apprenticeships in place so no one starts work knowing only a robot manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At fifty-three I may prefer teaching some days to storm callouts, but that is still paid work. Our mortgage may be smaller then, though I cannot assume it will be gone or that a training post will appear. A robot manual cannot teach an apprentice which power line to trust in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the apprenticeship coordinator this year for the assessor requirements and the pay band. If the company funds an assessor course on paid time and later posts a local trainer job covering our household costs, I would complete the course before 2036 and apply; I would keep line shifts until an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm about the long transition, while still careful with our present budget. I trust a decade of real apprenticeships more than a quick new title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you have apprentices do before using a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would make them find the isolation points on a real work site and explain the safe approach. Only then would I let them compare a machine’s route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a smaller trainer wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after my partner and I see the mortgage balance and actual hours at that time. I would not promise a cut today for a job that has not been posted.

say: A **decade** allows apprentices to learn real line repair before capable robots arrive around 2039.
I would **keep** practical site checks ahead of robot manuals.
think: A **paid** trainer job could reduce storm callouts if future family costs permit.
I **cannot** count on the mortgage disappearing or an unposted job appearing.
do: **Ask** coordinator for assessor requirements and trainer pay band this year.
**Complete** funded assessor course before 2036 if suitable local trainer job is posted.
**Apply** for local trainer job only if its pay covers future household costs.
feel: **Calmer** about the longer transition, still mindful of today’s mortgage.
S4.quote: A robot manual cannot teach an apprentice which power line to trust in the rain.
fieldNote: She **imagines** later teaching, not retirement, and keeps the mortgage condition explicit.
Her preference for established **apprenticeships** remains strong even in the slowest scenario, and she will keep field shifts until an offer exists.

steps.text: Complete funded assessor course before 2036 if suitable local trainer job posted
Apply for posted local trainer job if pay covers household costs
Keep line shifts until a suitable trainer offer exists

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots could be on the lines by around 2031 before the company has proved safe isolation or protected our callout hours. A paid human lead on every robot job and a written right to stop unsafe work would help. My line crew cannot be the final test of a machine bought on a promise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the apprentice to spot a bad work order. I learned that from an older lineworker before I had my diploma, and it has kept my crew out of trouble. The company should pay for that time if it wants careful workers.

headlineQuote: My line crew cannot be the final test of a machine bought on a promise.
portrait: **Daria** is a forty-three-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and strong judgment on physical line faults.
Her **typical** pay supports a partner, two school-age children and a mortgage, with one to six months of savings behind them.
She **avoids** AI tools, insists on signed isolation checks and measures new plans against actual work at the pole.
She **may** accept paid field inspection or apprenticeship teaching if a real local post meets household pay needs.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring capable robots onto power lines around 2031 before safe isolation and callout hours are protected.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid** human leads on robot jobs and written stop-work authority would help protect her crew and household wages.
